## Zero Trust Branch Routing Policies

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Articles/aSmPJ00000GdlAj0AJ/zero-trust-branch-routing-policies
- Type: Article

Article Details

Zero Trust SD-WAN

sashraf

(Employee) posted an Article

October 23, 2025 at 5:14 PM

Zero Trust Branch Routing Policies

Zero Trust Branch  routing policies enable organizations to control traffic from branch sites to specific destinations based on defined criteria, ensuring secure and optimized routing. These policies allow granular control over how traffic flows to Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA), Zscaler Private Access (ZPA), or directly to the Internet.

For more details, check the following link

Looking for practical answers to real-world technical questions?

Our

Technical Guides

area on Community highlights articles created by Zscaler experts in partnership with our Support teams, Solution Engineers, and Product teams. These guides are built to address the kinds of questions we see in the field, especially topics that may not make their way into the

Help site

, but are still incredibly valuable for customers, partners, and internal teams.

Here are just a few recent examples:

Cribl integration guide

Determine user count & peak transactions for an NSS virtual appliance deployment

## Zscaler MCP Server Installation and Integration Guide on MAC OS

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Articles/aSmPJ00000GeV770AF/zscaler-mcp-server-installation-and-integration-guide-on-mac-os
- Type: Article
- Last activity: 2026-06-24T14:31:28.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Article Details

Technical Guides

Ramesh M

(Employee) posted an Article

Edited June 24, 2026 at 2:31 PM

Zscaler MCP Server Installation and Integration Guide on MAC OS

Purpose

This document provides detailed step-by-step instructions to install the Zscaler MCP Server, configure OneAPI authentication, create environment variables, and integrate the MCP server with Claude Desktop and Codex on macOS.

Prerequisites

Tools : Python 3.12+, UV/UVX, Claude Desktop, Codex CLI

Required variables: Client ID, Client Secret, Customer ID, Vanity Domain.

Install UV and UVX

curl -LsSf

https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh

| sh

source ~/.zshrc

uv --version

uvx --version

which uvx

Create Environment File

touch ~/users/username/.env

nano ~/users/username/.env

Add:

ZSCALER_CLIENT_ID=YOUR_CLIENT_ID

ZSCALER_CLIENT_SECRET=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET

ZSCALER_CUSTOMER_ID=YOUR_CUSTOMER_ID

ZSCALER_VANITY_DOMAIN=VANITY DOMAIN

Install Zscaler MCP Server

uvx --env-file ~/.env zscaler-mcp

Expected: Initialising Zscaler Integrations MCP Server and Starting server with stdio transport.

Verify Entitlements

uvx --env-file ~/.env zscaler-mcp --debug

Expected: entitled services=[zcc, zdx, zia, zpa ] and tool registration counts.

Update the Zscaler MCP server

This compares your installed version against the latest release and reports whether an update is available.

uvx zscaler-mcp update

This verifies after upgrade

uvx zscaler-mcp –version

Refresh commands

uv tool upgrade zscaler-mcp

uvx --refresh zscaler-mcp –version

Configure Claude Desktop

Open ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json and add MCP server configuration with uvx, env-file and services zia,zpa,zdx,zcc.

“mcpServers”: {

"zscaler": {

“command": /Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.12/bin/uvx",

"args": [

"--env-file",

"/Users/ramesh/.env",

"zscaler-mcp",

"--services",

"zia,zpa,zdx,zcc,ztw,zid,zeasm,zins,zms",

"--enable-write-tools",

"--write-tools",

"zpa_*,zia_*,zdx_*,zcc_*,ztw_*,zid_*,zeasm_*,zins_*,zms_*"

},

Verify Claude Integration

Ask Claude: List available ZIA tools, Show first 10 ZIA users, List ZPA App Connectors.

Configure Codex

If the file does not exist

mkdir -p ~/.codex

Create ~/.codex/config.toml

Codex TOML Example

[mcp_servers.zscaler]

command = "uvx"

args = [

"--env-file",

"/Users/ramesh/.env",

"zscaler-mcp",

"--services",

"zia,zpa,zdx,zcc,ztw,zid,zeasm,zins,zms",

"--enable-write-tools",

"--write-tools",

"zpa_*,zia_*,zdx_*,zcc_*,ztw_*,zid_*,zeasm_*,zins_*,zms_*"

enabled = true

startup_timeout_sec = 60

tool_timeout_sec = 300

Verify Codex Integration

Start codex and ask: List available MCP tools, List ZIA users, List ZPA Application Segments.

Troubleshooting

No environment file found

-> verify ~/.env. 401 Unauthorized

-> verify OAuth details. Auth URL misconfiguration

-> use vanity domain only. ZIA tools missing

-> use --services zia,zpa,zdx,zcc.

## 3rd Party / Contractors - How to protect data from Mobile / Personal Laptop ?

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Blogs/aSnPJ00000001CD0AY/3rd-party-contractors-how-to-protect-data-from-mobile-personal-laptop-
- Type: Blog
- Last activity: 2025-05-09T18:42:31.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Blog Details

Zscalerzerotrustbrowser

mohamed.e

(Employee) posted a Blog

Edited May 9, 2025 at 6:42 PM

3rd Party / Contractors - How to protect data from Mobile / Personal Laptop ?

Zscaler Zero Trust Browser

Organizations often need to provide access to internal or sanctioned SaaS applications to contractors or employees using unmanaged devices or BYOD. However, this creates an avenue for data leak as there is very little control that the organization has over this traffic. This results in a huge gap between the security cover provided to protect the applications and data when being accessed from a managed endpoint vs. an unmanaged endpoint.

In most cases a managed endpoint is configured to forward traffic via the Zscaler Zero Trust Exchange, by the help of a Zscaler Client Connector or an alternative forwarding method. This ensures that all the defined security policies such as Data leak policies, Access Control policies or security policies are enforced on the application accessed, thus providing full control and visibility of the traffic to the organization. However, in case of an unmanaged device, the organization has little to no control over the end machine, thus forwarding the traffic via Zscaler Zero trust exchange challenging.

The solution described in this document allows an organization to configure the different components of the Zscaler Zero Trust Exchange (ZTNA) such as ZIA, ZPA and Isolation, enabling it to extend the same level of security cover offered to a managed device to an unmanaged device as well, while accessing sanctioned SaaS applications or internal application.This proposed solution is designed to allows an organization to extend access to web based SaaS and private applications via an isolated containerized browser which is configured to forward traffic via the Zscaler Zero trust exchange (ZIA and ZPA), while blocking access to the SaaS applications from unmanaged devices using the conditional access capabilities of their Identity Provider (IdP).

Are you Interested to know more ?

Demo is Here.

#zscalerzerotrustbrowser

## Redeploying Virtual Service Edges with existing IP addresses

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000063Hl0AI/redeploying-virtual-service-edges-with-existing-ip-addresses
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-07-22T07:00:29.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited 5h ago

Redeploying Virtual Service Edges with existing IP addresses

Note:

Special thanks to

Andres Garcia D'Alta

for their contributions to this guide.

If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

This guide provides instructions on how to redeploy your Zscaler Virtual Service Edge (VSE) while maintaining your existing Internet Protocol (IP) addresses. This process is necessary when upgrading certain VSE(s) from Zscaler Operating System 24 (ZSOS24) to ZSOS42.

Prerequisites

Confirm support for the platform you want the new VSE to run on and follow the VSE deployment guide for your platform. Review the following documentation for more details:

Virtual Service Edge.

Confirm resource requirements: 48 GB RAM minimum for the new VSE image. Ensure CPU and storage align with the sizing guidance.

Download the Zscaler provided migration script from the comments section. This script should be uploaded to the new VSE before migration with a tool such as SCP.

Preparing for redeployment

1) Back up the existing VSE settings and reference details

In the ESXi host, collect screenshots of:

Network adapter details as shown by the hypervisor (interface order, assigned networks/ Virtual Local Area Networks, Media Access Control (MAC), IP/mask, gateway and Domain Name System (DNS)

Run the following following commands on the existing VSE and capture the output:

crontab -l > /sc/cronjobs_24

ifconfig -a > /sc/update/vzen_ifconfig_output_24.txt

2) If you use an Secured Sockets Layer (SSL) Acceleration/ nitrox card for the old VSE:

Make sure you rebuild the new VSE in a hypervisor that has access to the card.

Deploy a VSE reusing the existing IPs using Zscaler’s provided migration script

If you are migrating a standalone VSE and do not wish to have a service disruption during migration, establish a temporary

GRE

or

IPsec

tunnel to Zscaler and redirect workload traffic to that tunnel during the migration window.

Note:

If you are migrating a cluster VSE, plan node-by-node deployment to maintain service during the migration.

Shut down existing VSE

In the ESXi host, make a copy of the .vmdk file of the existing VSE and keep it as a backup

Download the latest VSE image from the Zscaler Admin UI

Create the new VSE virtual machine with this new image.

In the hypervisor (ESXi), assign the same network configuration from existing VSE (MAC and IP) addresses to the new VSE network interfaces.

Attach the old VSE disk to this newly created VM

click on vm settings

Then select "Add new device"

Now select "existing hard disk"

Select the Datastore where your old VSE is present and select the .vmdk file from your old VSE directory.

Power on the new VSE instance.

Validate network settings like MAC and IP address assignment by running "ifconfig -a" on the new VSE

Run gpart show -l command to obtain the disk name of the old VSE. This disk name will be used in Zscaler’s provided script

E.g: In the below case "da0" is the default disk of the new VSE (ZSOS42) and "da1s1" is the old VSE disk (ZSOS24)

so old_disk_name is "da1s1"

Download migration script from the comment below and place it in /sc path

Execute the following command under /sc path :

bash vzen_zos42_redeploy_helper.sh -a -b -d -m [Ex: old_disk_name is "da1s1"]

E.g: bash vzen_zos42_redeploy_helper.sh -a -b -d

da1s1

-m

The script initially copies the required conf files from old_disk_name, then it will proceed with moving all the ZSOS24 /sc contents to ZSOS42 disk.

Script Explanation:

# bash vzen_zerotouch_redeployment.sh -b --disk /dev/ [--after_action] [--existing ] [–skip] [--move_sc] [–disk_attached_manually]

# -b : backup mode

# --disk/-d : old disk partition name.

# --after_action/-a : perform after move (or) download actions automatically.

# --existing/-e : existing backup archive to use for restoring config. (use this when backup archive is already available)

# --skip/-s : skip applying config files to new VZEN (This will skip copying rc.conf, snmpd.conf, ntp.conf, resolv.conf from Old VSE to New)

# --move_sc/-m : move /sc data from old disk to new VZEN instance and perform post redeployment actions (Keep this flag when you attached your old disk to new VZEN)

# --disk_attached_manually/-n : check "common issues 1", if you encounter that scenario please use this.

Note

The whole process will take approximately 40m to 2hrs depending on disk I/O speeds. Zscaler recommends planning for 3 hrs.

Below is an example of the expected output from the script:

Expected Output :

Note:

Added Missing keys

might differ for your VSE.

Post "Redeployment completed successfully" message, run a dif between /etc/rc.conf and /mnt/etc/rc.conf to validate that all settings have been properly copied from the old VSE to the new VSE

Validate status and basic health on the new VSE

VSE status

Run "sudo vzen status"

Migration and traffic processing validation

If you have an SSL/nitrox card execute the following commands:

vzen stop

vzen install-nitrox

vzen start

If snmp is enabled, execute following commands to validate

service snmpd status

service snmpd start ( if status is not running )

snmpwalk -v3 -u vzensnmp -l authPriv -a SHA -A vzensnmp -x AES -X vzensnmp localhost .1.3.6.1.4.1.46262.9.2.1

The above command should return an output without error.

If you use a temporary GRE/IPsec tunnel, redirect traffic back from the tunnel to the VSE.

Monitor traffic and ZIA logs.

Confirm that clients can reach intended destinations through the VSE; expected policies are applied.

Decommission the old VSE

Decommission it once the new VSE is stable.

Common issues

Sometimes when the script tries to mount an old disk to the new VSE, we may encounter failed scenarios saying "Failed to mount old disk ......."

In this scenario, we need to find and attach the partitions manually by executing ` mount /dev/da1s1a /mnt ; mount /dev/da1s1e /mnt/usr ; mount /dev/da1s1g /mnt/sc ; mount /dev/da1s1f /mnt/var `.

Once it's is completed, now run the script again with these options `bash vzen_zos42_redeploy_helper.sh -a -b -n -m`.

Moving '/sc' data from old_disk to new VSE might fail with the error message "Failed to move /sc data", in this case you can re-run the script with the following arguments

get the existing archive from '/var/tmp' directory with naming /var/tmp/zvmbackup_.tar.gz

bash vzen_zos42_redeploy_helper.sh -a -m -e

/var/tmp/zvmbackup_.tar.gz

If moving files fails multiple times, please run above command by removing -m option

Eg: bash vzen_zos42_redeploy_helper.sh -a -e

/var/tmp/zvmbackup_.tar.gz

If you can’t SSH to the node, please execute the following from console "service netif restart" and "service routing restart" and "service sshd restart"

Roll back procedure

If you encounter issues during the redeployment and need to roll back to the old VSE, please try the following steps:

Shut down the new VSE VM

Detach the old VSE disk from the new VSE VM

Turn on the old VSE VM and confirm that clients can reach intended destinations through the VSE; expected policies are applied.

Please reach out to us in the comments section if you have any questions.

Farooq

(Customer)

2 months ago

crontab -l > /sc/cronjobs_24 throws an error

crontab: no crontab for zsroot

Andres Garcia

(Employee)

2 months ago

Looks like you are executing the command from zsroot user. You should run all the commands from root user space. Thanks!

Yashraj Singha

(Employee)

5h ago

July 22, 2026

The updated script can be downloaded here.

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000063uT0AQ/various-rule-action-options-available-in-the-client-forwarding-policy-page","lastmod":"2026-03-03T16:27:39.000Z","id":"aSoPJ00000063uT0AQ"} -->
## Various “Rule Action” options available in the Client Forwarding Policy page

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000063uT0AQ/various-rule-action-options-available-in-the-client-forwarding-policy-page
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-03-03T16:27:39.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited March 3, 2026 at 4:27 PM

Various “Rule Action” options available in the Client Forwarding Policy page

Note:

Special thanks to

Raj Kumar

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance.

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction:

ZPA Client Forwarding Policy allows you to control which applications segment definitions get downloaded to the client, and how the client behaves.

Solution:

When you define a client forwarding policy, you have 3 actions that can be applied to an application segment:

Forward to ZPA

Bypass ZPA

Only Forward Allowed Applications

Refer to the documentation

Configuring Client Forwarding Policies

for more details.

Forward to ZPA

It allows all the configured application segments to be downloaded to the client, which will forward the applications to ZPA cloud, where policy will be applied. For example, consider the application segment, centos.welshgeek.net:80. The user will initiate the DNS query, and the Zscaler Client Connector (ZCC) will intercept the DNS request and resolve it to 100.64.0.0/16 address. The client would connect to the IP address on port 80 and traffic is forwarded to the ZPA cloud for the policy to be applied.

Bypass ZPA

It allows the application segment to be downloaded to the client, but also tells the client to not send them to ZPA. The client will bypass ZPA for such applications

Only Forward Allowed Applications

By enabling this option, the Access Policy is evaluated first before downloading the application segments on client machine. Only Allowed application segments for that particular user are downloaded on the client machine. For example, consider the application segment, centos.welshgeek.net:80. Also, consider that user

mryan@welshgeek.net

is denied access, while user

bob@welshgeek.net

is allowed access in the access policy.

When user

mryan@welshgeek.net

requests the application, it will not have a definition for the application and hence would attempt to "

go direct

". When user

bob@welshgeek.net

requests the application, ZCC will intercept the DNS request and resolve it to 100.64.0.0/16 address. The client would connect to the IP address on port 80 and traffic is forwarded to the ZPA cloud for the policy to be applied.

However, there are two important considerations to the "

Only Forward Allowed Applications

" option to plan in your application segment policy:

In the above example, the user

mryan@welshgeek.net

is denied access to the application and hence would not be able to download the application segment. However, if there is a wildcard application segment (*.welshgeek.net) which is defined for the user to download, when the user attempts to access centos.welshgeek.net:80, this would match against the *.welshgeek.net wildcard discovery application segment. The traffic would then be intercepted and forwarded to the ZPA cloud, where the policy would apply and deny access to the application. If the expectation is for this application to bypass ZPA, then this would not be the outcome. A separate application segment needs to be created for a specific app segment to be bypassed.

DNS SRV records however return pointers to services (example: _ldap._tcp.welshgeek.net returns a pointer to domain: controller.welshgeek.net:389). The DNS would still match the wildcard discovery and return the answer to the user. In some cases (example: MS Teams/Skype uses _sip._tls.welshgeek.net.) you might explicitly want this to bypass and resolve to the internet. In such cases, you should use a bypass policy rather than the

Only Forward Allowed Applications

option.

Careful consideration is necessary to get the desired outcome when using "

Only Forward Allowed Applications

" policy when combined with a wildcard discovery application segment.

This video

provides working examples of the behaviors and the outcomes of different policies.

Why the default policy action is "Forward to ZPA" rather than "Only Forward Allowed Applications"?

It was primarily an historical decision from Zscaler to emulate through the default policy action, a behavior similar to a Full tunnel VPN setup: any App Segment defined under ZPA will capture traffic towards ZPA, regardless of Access Policy outcome.

Greenfield ZPA customers typically want to start with wildcard domain App Segments and very few generic access policies, then discover the applications and later in the implementation process, start to deny access or have more fine-grained Access Policies per User Groups. This type of phased ZPA implementation is possible only if the default policy action is

"Forward to ZPA"

and would be harder to troubleshoot initially with a default action of

"Only Forward Allowed Applications"

The default policy action can be changed to "Only Forward Allowed Applications” as well. You need to ensure that this would not impact your current operations with Application discovery and Access Policy troubleshooting: switching to

Only

Forward

Allowed

Applications

“will have the effect of evaluating the Access Policies first before downloading the App Segments to ZCC.

Compared to

"Forward to ZPA"

action, this means that you might not get some of the logs / app discovery related to users accessing a ZPA application rather than getting rejected by the Access Policy.

With

"Forward to ZPA"

action the user is forwarded to ZPA for all App Segments and then the Access Policy is evaluated.

Pros of having "Forward to ZPA" as the default policy action

It provides detailed logs for

access denied

scenarios. This could be useful for tuning the ZPA Access Policies and troubleshooting why a user is getting denied access.

The ZPA admin portal

Dashboard

Application

section is also populated for applications being denied by Access Policies.

Cons of having "Forward to ZPA" as the default policy action

The users cannot access some local domains/IP addresses that match ZPA App Segment definitions.

Please reach out to us in the comments section if you have any questions.

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000063zJ0AQ/how-to-collect-packet-capture-and-journal-logs-on-docker-app-connector","lastmod":"2026-03-06T20:27:36.000Z","id":"aSoPJ00000063zJ0AQ"} -->
## How to collect Packet Capture and Journal Logs on Docker App Connector?

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000063zJ0AQ/how-to-collect-packet-capture-and-journal-logs-on-docker-app-connector
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-03-06T20:27:36.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Cd

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited March 6, 2026 at 8:27 PM

How to collect Packet Capture and Journal Logs on Docker App Connector?

Note:

Special thanks to

Subhrajit Mahi

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance.

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction:

This article explains how to collect packet captures (PCAPs) and Docket container logs for the Zscaler App Connector. These files are essential for troubleshooting network traffic and container performance issues.

Note: You must run these commands on the Docket host itself, not within the container.

Solution:

Packet Capture Collection (Docket Host):

Identify the Network Interface:

Run the following command on the Docket host to list available interfaces:

> ip link show

This command shows interface names (not IP assignments details

Note down the adapter name responsible for the traffic (example: ens5)

Capture traffic to a Specific Destination Host:

Use tcpdump to capture traffic destined to a particular host:

> sudo tcpdump -i -nves0 -w /tmp/zscaler.pcap host

Where:

is the interface identified earlier (example: ens5)

is the target host you want to filter on (example: google.com)

Output file will be saved as: /tmp/zscaler.pcap

Refer to this example:

sudo tcpdump -i ens5 -nves0 -w /tmp/zscaler.pcap host

google.com

If the correct interface cannot be identified:

If you are unsure which interfact is carry the traffic, capture on all interfaces, use this command:

> sudo tcpdump -i any -nves0 -w /tmp/zscaler.pcap host

google.com

Open (Unflitered) packet capture: To run an open capture (no destination filter), use this command:

> sudo tcpdump -i any nves0 -w /tmp/zscaler.pcap

Note: Open packet captures can generate large files quickly. Stop the capture once you reproduce the issue.

Logs Collection (Docket Host):

Refer to the following command to see running container on docker:

> sudo docket ps -a

Once you have the container ID of the App Connector:

View Recent Logs (Last 50 lines):

To quickly review recent container logs, use the following command:

> sudo docket logs --tail 50

Follow Logs in Real Time:

To stream logs live, use this command:

> sudo docker logs -f

Export Logs with Timestamps to a File:

To export logs with timestamps into a file for sharing, use this command: > sudo docket logs -t > /tmp/log.txt

Outputs Collected:

Packet capture file: /tmp/zscaler.pcap

Docker logs file (optional export): /tmp/log.txt

You can view the file by using these commands:

#cd /tmp

#ls

It will show you the captured file. You can use winscp or other tools to export the collected log files from the docket host.

Please reach out to us in the comments section if you have any questions.

## Check and manually update the Virtual Service Edge build version

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000064tl0AA/check-and-manually-update-the-virtual-service-edge-build-version
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-03-06T13:37:35.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Vzen

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

March 6, 2026 at 1:37 PM

Check and manually update the Virtual Service Edge build version

Note:

Special thanks to

Diego Marin Hernand

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance.

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction:

Keeping your Zscaler Virtual Service Edge™ (VSE) up to date is essential for maintaining the security and performance of your network. While updates typically happen automatically, there are times when you may need to verify the current build or manually trigger an upgrade to ensure you are running the latest software.

In some cases, the Virtual Service Edge service build may not upgrade automatically during the scheduled window. You might notice a mismatch between the installed version and the latest available version when checking the server status.

Automatic updates can occasionally fail due to network interruptions or internal synchronization issues. When the installed version does not match the latest available build branch, a manual update is required to bring the node into compliance with the latest release.

Solution:

First, you need to identify which version is currently installed and compare it to what is available on the update server.

Use SSH to log in to the Virtual Service Edge server.

Check the latest available software version by running the following command:

sudo vzen checkversion

Note: In some of the previous scenarios where the installed version and the latest available version do not match, even after manually performing an update on the Virtual Service Edge use the command:

sudo vzen update-now or sudo vzen force-update

Use the following command to check the build installed on the node:

/sc/sme/bin/sme -V.

Output

[ vse00 ]#/sc/sme/bin/sme -V

//+SHARED MEMORY KEY 17 (/sc/sme/)

sme: version 6.2r.2509_prod107.9.195007956_114

Running the

sudo vezen checkversion

command may reveal that the installed build version is different from the latest available build version

Output

[ vse00 ]#vzen checkversion

//+SHARED MEMORY KEY 17 (/sc/smcdsc/)

Connecting to update server x.x.x.x

Downloaded build version: 195007956

Latest available build version: 195007956

Installed build version sme: 6225091079

Installed build version smcdsc: 6225091079

Installed build version smlb: 6225091079

Available switch versions: 6225087511, 6225087517, 6225091079

The version numbers are generated as follows:

Latest available build version

: 195007956 - This corresponds to the second part of the build version: 195007956_114.

Installed build version (SME)

: 6225091079 - This corresponds to the first part of the build branch: 6.2r.2509_prod107.9.

Output

[ vse00 ]#/sc/sme/bin/sme -V

//+SHARED MEMORY KEY 17 (/sc/sme/)

sme: version 6.2r.2509_prod107.9.195007956_114

Hence, in this case, if the installed version matches the latest available version as shown by the output of the

/sc/sme/bin/sme -V

command, the VZEN will be running the latest available version.

If the "

Installed build version

" and "

Latest available build version

" do not match, update manually using the following commands:

sudo vzen update-now

sudo vzen force-update-now

Once the update commands are executed and the Virtual Service Edge comes back up, run the following command to restart Virtual Service Edge service:

sudo vzen restart

Check the latest build version using the following command:

sudo vzen checkversion

Verify all the services are running using the following command:

sudo vzen status

Refer to the documentation

Troubleshooting Virtual Service Edges

for more details.

Please reach out to us in the comments section if you have any questions.

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000065Hx0AI/generate-custom-root-ca-for-zpa-log-streaming-service","lastmod":"2026-03-11T17:47:24.000Z","id":"aSoPJ00000065Hx0AI"} -->
## Generate custom Root CA for ZPA Log Streaming Service

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000065Hx0AI/generate-custom-root-ca-for-zpa-log-streaming-service
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-03-11T17:47:24.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited March 11, 2026 at 5:47 PM

Generate custom Root CA for ZPA Log Streaming Service

Note:

Special thanks to

Shivprasad Tiwari

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance.

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

To enhance the security of your Log Streaming Service (LSS) for Zscaler Private Access, you can enable Transport Layer Security (TLS) for encrypted communication. This process involves generating a custom Root Certificate Authority (CA) using OpenSSL on a Windows client, then creating and uploading custom certificates to your ZPA tenant and Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) tool. This article guides you through the necessary steps to set up a custom Root CA and enable TLS for your ZPA Log Streaming Service.

Installing OpenSSL on a Windows Client

To begin, you will need to install OpenSSL on your Windows client machine to generate the necessary certificates.

Download OpenSSL:

Download a compatible Windows distribution of OpenSSL from a trusted source

here

Install OpenSSL:

Follow the installation wizard to install the application on your system.

Locate Installation Directory

: Once installed, navigate to the OpenSSL installation directory. Typically, this might be C:\Program Files\OpenSSL-Win64\bin. Copy this path.

Add to System Path:

Search for view advanced system settings in Windows and open it.

Click on Environment Variables....

Under System variables, find and select Path, then click Edit....

Click New and paste the OpenSSL binary directory path (e.g., C:\Program Files\OpenSSL-Win64\bin)

Move this new entry to the top of the list for priority and click OK to save all settings.

Verify Installation:

Open a new Command Prompt window and type openssl version. You should see output similar to this, indicating a successful installation:

Generating a Custom Root CA and Uploading to ZPA

With OpenSSL installed, you can now generate your private key and self-signed Root CA certificate.

Generate Private Key:

Open Command Prompt and run the following command to generate a 4096-bit RSA private key named root key:

openssl genrsa -out root.key 4096

Generate Root CA Certificate:

Next, run the following command to create your self-signed Root CA certificate (root.crt). Replace "Test CA 1" with a descriptive name for your Certificate Authority. This certificate will be valid for 3650 days. (approximately 10 years)

openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -key root.key -subj "/CN=Test CA 1" -sha256 -days 3650 -out root.crt

Upload Root CA to ZPA:

Log in to the ZPA Admin Portal.

Navigate to Configuration & Control > Certificate Management > Enrollment Certificates.

Click Actions > Upload Certificate Chain.

Follow the prompts to upload your root.crt file.

Generating a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) in ZPA

After uploading your Root CA, you need to generate a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) from the ZPA Admin Portal. This CSR will be used to obtain your custom certificate.

Navigate to Certificates:

In the ZPA Admin Portal, navigate to Configuration & Control > Certificate Management > Enrollment Certificates.

Create CSR:

Click Actions > Create CSR.

Download CSR:

Complete the fields for the CSR and then download the generated .csr file. This file contains the public key and other information needed to request a certificate from your Root CA.

Generating and Uploading the Custom Certificate

Now, you will use the downloaded CSR, along with your Root CA's private key and certificate, to generate the actual custom certificate.

Generate Custom Certificate:

Open Command Prompt and run the following command. Replace testlss.csr with the name of the CSR file you downloaded from ZPA™, and test.crt with your desired certificate name. This command uses your root.key and root.crt to sign the CSR, creating your new custom certificate. This certificate will be valid for 365 days.

openssl x509 -req -in testlss.csr -CA root.crt -CAkey root.key -CAcreateserial -out test.crt -days 365 -sha256 -copy_extensions copyall

Upload Custom Certificate to ZPA:

Return to the ZPA Admin Portal, in the Enrollment Certificates section.

Locate the pending CSR entry for which you just generated the certificate.

Click on the entry and follow the prompts to upload the test.crt file you just created.

Once the certificate is uploaded successfully, it will be visible in the ZPA Admin Portal, showing its status and details.

Deploying the Log Receiver with TLS Enabled

With your custom certificate uploaded and active in ZPA, you are now ready to deploy your ZPA Log Streaming Service with TLS encryption.

Deploy Log Receiver:

When deploying or configuring your Log Receiver in ZPA, you can now select the new custom certificate you just uploaded. This tells ZPA to use this certificate for establishing TLS connections.

Upload Certificate to SIEM Tool:

For end-to-end TLS encryption, you must also upload the same test.crt (your custom certificate) to your SIEM tool or log receiver application. This allows your SIEM to trust the connection from ZPA and decrypt the incoming logs.

By following these steps, you ensure that log data streamed from ZPA to your SIEM tool is encrypted using TLS, providing enhanced security and data integrity.

Please reach out to us in the comments section if you have any questions.

## How to Failover ZPA Traffic?

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000065bJ0AQ/how-to-failover-zpa-traffic
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-03-25T13:47:04.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Fff

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited March 25, 2026 at 1:47 PM

How to Failover ZPA Traffic?

Note:

Special thanks to

Priyanka B C

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

This article provides a structured, step-by-step procedure to fail over Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) traffic when the primary path is degraded or unavailable. Following these steps helps you minimize service disruption by managing failovers for Service Edge, regional hubs, App Connectors, and Zscaler Private Service Edge (PSE) instances. This guide applies to production failovers caused by path degradation from Internet Service Providers (ISPs), data centers (DCs), regional backbones, or specific Zscaler infrastructure issues.

Solution

ZPA traffic path overview

To effectively fail over traffic, it is helpful to understand the high-level path:

[User] → [ZPA Broker/Service Edge] → [App Connector] → [Private App]

Pre-Checks

Before initiating a failover, perform the following steps to ensure you have the necessary data and approvals:

Confirm the scope of the impact (e.g., is it a single site, a specific region, or a global issue?).

Verify that your Forwarding Profile has Dynamic latency-based Service Edge selection enabled.

Collect evidence of the degradation:

Client to Service Edge: Check latency and packet loss using MTR or traceroute.

App Connector to Service Edge: Check latency and packet loss using MTR or traceroute.

Review the health of your App Connectors and Private Service Edges in the ZPA Admin Portal.

Identify the primary and secondary Broker or Service Edge regions currently in use based on your policy behavior.

Ensure you have a change approval and a rollback plan ready, especially if you are moving App Connector groups.

Quick Decision Guide

Use the following table to determine which failover scenario fits your current situation:

Scenario

When to use

Service Edge / Broker Failover

Degradation is isolated to a single ZPA DC, Broker, or Service Edge (e.g., localized ISP incident).

Regional Failover

Multiple ZPA DCs are impacted across an entire region (e.g., regional backbone or exchange incident).

App Connector Failover

The App Connector path is degraded, or the connector is at capacity, even if Brokers appear healthy.

Private Service Edge Failover

Degradation is isolated to your internal PSE infrastructure.

ZPA Business Continuity

Used only during catastrophic Zscaler service failures.

Scenario 1: Service Edge / Broker / DC Failover

Use this scenario when issues are isolated to a single ZPA Broker, Service Edge, or DC.

Failover steps

Prefer automatic failover: Ensure Dynamic latency-based Service Edge selection is enabled in the Forwarding Profile. This allows Zscaler Client Connector (ZCC) to automatically select the healthiest Service Edge based on latency.

Note: If you do not see the Dynamic Latency-based configuration option, or if the feature is not working as expected, please contact Zscaler Support for assistance.

Manual fallback: If automation is insufficient, engage Zscaler Support to temporarily remove or deprioritize the impacted DC for your tenant.

Validate on clients: ZPA service edge changes require a service restart on the client to take effect. You can do this in two ways:

Open Zscaler Client Connector, go to More > Diagnostics, and click Restart Service.

Open Zscaler Client Connector, go to Private Access, and toggle the Service Status Off and then On.

Validation checklist

Retest application access and observe the new Service Edge region assignment.

Confirm symptoms have cleared for affected users.

Verify reduced round-trip time (RTT) or packet loss to the new Broker.

Ensure application transaction success rates have returned to normal.

Rollback

When the DC or Broker is confirmed healthy, restore the default selection and remove any temporary exclusions.

Scenario 2: Performing a regional failover

Use this scenario if there is widespread impact across all ZPA DCs in a specific region, such as a regional backbone failure.

Note

: If you have alternate App Connectors (ACs) or Private Service Edges (PSEs) hosted in a region different from that of your users, leverage the documented failover scenarios for ACs and PSEs.

Example:

A subsea cable cut between India and the US causes congestion. India users access applications fronted by ACs in the US, resulting in high latency. If you have ACs in Singapore or Kuala Lumpur, update the ZPA configuration so only those ACs serve India user traffic. Traffic will then route India User → India Broker → Singapore AC → US App (instead of India → US), avoiding the congested path. Similarly, if you have PSEs in Singapore, reroute through the Singapore PSE rather than the impacted data center. Traffic will then route India User → Singapore PSE → US AC → US App (instead of India → US)

Failover steps

Steer users to a non-impacted region. This happens automatically when dynamic selection is enabled by excluding impacted DCs where latency exceeds the configured threshold.

If manual intervention is needed, contact Zscaler Support to exclude regional DCs for your tenant.

Retest connectivity. If the problem persists, validate the path in both directions:

Client to Service Edge (via MTR or traceroute).

App Connector to Service Edge (via MTR or traceroute).

Note: You can use the Zscaler Support information tool or log into the App Connector to capture packet traces and validate latency.

If the Broker-to-Connector path still shows loss, adjust your App Connector groups to a healthy region:

Shift your access policies or segment groups to App Connector groups in a healthy region.

Ensure the new region has enough capacity for the redirected user base.

Validation checklist

Confirm clients are resolving to Service Edges in the alternate region.

Verify that RTT metrics are acceptable from both the client and App Connector vantage points.

Confirm target applications are reachable with expected performance.

Rollback

Re-enable the original regional footprint once the backbone or regional incident is resolved.

Scenario 3: Failing over App Connectors

Use this scenario when application degradation is caused by App Connector location, capacity, or the transit path to the Broker.

Failover steps

Confirm Connector-side symptoms, such as high CPU/memory usage or elevated packet loss between the App Connector and the Service Edge.

Fail over to healthy App Connector groups by reassigning the relevant application segments or policies to alternate groups, preferably in a non-impacted region.

Validate internal routing and allowlists, including firewalls, DNS, and service discovery for the new path.

Perform a capacity check to ensure the destination App Connector group has enough headroom for sessions and network throughput.

Validation checklist

Verify App Connector health is green in the ZPA Admin Portal.

Confirm no persistent packet loss to the selected Service Edge.

Ensure application transactions are successful from client devices.

Rollback

Restore the original App Connector groups once the primary path is validated as stable.

Scenario 4: Failing over Zscaler Private Service Edge

Use this scenario when the degradation is isolated to your PSE infrastructure.

Failover steps

Validate PSE health in the ZPA Admin Portal and review resource consumption.

Steer traffic away from the impacted PSE:

Temporarily direct traffic via the Zscaler cloud path if your policy allows.

Fail over to an alternate PSE site or cluster.

Confirm reachability and policy alignment for the alternate path.

Validation checklist

Confirm sessions are established via the alternate PSE or cloud path without errors.

Verify acceptable latency and throughput for critical applications.

Rollback

Return traffic to the primary PSE once stability and performance are verified.

Note:

Make sure to document all temporary constellation or policy changes with clear owners and expiry/review times. All changes to the primary path should be reverted once the incident is resolved. If symptoms persist after failover, escalate to Zscaler Support with all relevant information.

Please reach out to us in the comments section if you have any questions.

GordonWright

(Customer)

4 months ago

You need to have these features enabled in your tenant otherwise you get intermittent results, especially for ZPA.

Priyanka_BC

(Customer)

4 months ago

Good callout, thanks ! "Dynamic latency-based Service Edge selection" is one such feature which needs to be explicitly enabled for the tenant and configured under ZCC App Profile But most of the other configuration steps mentioned here aren't governed by feature flags.

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000065zV0AQ/various-rule-action-options-available-in-the-client-forwarding-policy-page","lastmod":"2026-04-01T10:14:44.000Z","id":"aSoPJ00000065zV0AQ"} -->
## Various “Rule Action” options available in the Client Forwarding Policy page

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000065zV0AQ/various-rule-action-options-available-in-the-client-forwarding-policy-page
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-04-01T10:14:44.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

ZDX - ZIA

Anamika_R

(Employee) posted a Guide

April 1, 2026 at 10:14 AM

Various “Rule Action” options available in the Client Forwarding Policy page

Note: Special thanks to Raj Kumar for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance.

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction:

ZPA Client Forwarding Policy allows you to control which applications segment definitions get downloaded to the client, and how the client behaves.

Solution:

When you define a client forwarding policy, you have 3 actions that can be applied to an application segment:

Forward to ZPA

Bypass ZPA

Only Forward Allowed Applications

Refer to the documentation Configuring Client Forwarding Policies for more details.

Forward to ZPA:

It allows all the configured application segments to be downloaded to the client, which will forward the applications to ZPA cloud, where policy will be applied. For example, consider the application segment, centos.welshgeek.net:80. The user will initiate the DNS query, and the Zscaler Client Connector (ZCC) will intercept the DNS request and resolve it to 100.64.0.0/16 address. The client would connect to the IP address on port 80 and traffic is forwarded to the ZPA cloud for the policy to be applied.

Bypass ZPA:

It allows the application segment to be downloaded to the client, but also tells the client to not send them to ZPA. The client will bypass ZPA for such applications

Only Forward Allowed Applications:

By enabling this option, the Access Policy is evaluated first before downloading the application segments on client machine. Only Allowed application segments for that particular user are downloaded on the client machine. For example, consider the application segment, centos.welshgeek.net:80. Also, consider that user

mryan@welshgeek.net

is denied access, while user

bob@welshgeek.net

is allowed access in the access policy.

When user

mryan@welshgeek.net

requests the application, it will not have a definition for the application and hence would attempt to "go direct". When user

bob@welshgeek.net

requests the application, ZCC will intercept the DNS request and resolve it to 100.64.0.0/16 address. The client would connect to the IP address on port 80 and traffic is forwarded to the ZPA cloud for the policy to be applied.

However, there are two important considerations to the "Only Forward Allowed Applications" option to plan in your application segment policy:

In the above example, the user

mryan@welshgeek.net

is denied access to the application and hence would not be able to download the application segment. However, if there is a wildcard application segment (*.welshgeek.net) which is defined for the user to download, when the user attempts to access centos.welshgeek.net:80, this would match against the *.welshgeek.net wildcard discovery application segment. The traffic would then be intercepted and forwarded to the ZPA cloud, where the policy would apply and deny access to the application. If the expectation is for this application to bypass ZPA, then this would not be the outcome. A separate application segment needs to be created for a specific app segment to be bypassed.

DNS SRV records however return pointers to services (example: _ldap._tcp.welshgeek.net returns a pointer to domain: controller.welshgeek.net:389). The DNS would still match the wildcard discovery and return the answer to the user. In some cases (example: MS Teams/Skype uses _sip._tls.welshgeek.net.) you might explicitly want this to bypass and resolve to the internet. In such cases, you should use a bypass policy rather than the “Only Forward Allowed Applications” option.

Careful consideration is necessary to get the desired outcome when using "Only Forward Allowed Applications" policy when combined with a wildcard discovery application segment. This video provides working examples of the behaviors and the outcomes of different policies.

Why the default policy action is "Forward to ZPA" rather than "Only Forward Allowed Applications"?

It was primarily an historical decision from Zscaler to emulate through the default policy action, a behavior similar to a Full tunnel VPN setup: any App Segment defined under ZPA will capture traffic towards ZPA, regardless of Access Policy outcome.

Greenfield ZPA customers typically want to start with wildcard domain App Segments and very few generic access policies, then discover the applications and later in the implementation process, start to deny access or have more fine-grained Access Policies per User Groups. This type of phased ZPA implementation is possible only if the default policy action is "Forward to ZPA" and would be harder to troubleshoot initially with a default action of "Only Forward Allowed Applications".

The default policy action can be changed to "Only Forward Allowed Applications” as well. You need to ensure that this would not impact your current operations with Application discovery and Access Policy troubleshooting: switching to "Only Forward Allowed Applications “will have the effect of evaluating the Access Policies first before downloading the App Segments to ZCC.

Compared to "Forward to ZPA" action, this means that you might not get some of the logs / app discovery related to users accessing a ZPA application rather than getting rejected by the Access Policy.

With "Forward to ZPA" action the user is forwarded to ZPA for all App Segments and then the Access Policy is evaluated.

Pros of having "Forward to ZPA" as the default policy action:

It provides detailed logs for ‘access denied’ scenarios. This could be useful for tuning the ZPA Access Policies and troubleshooting why a user is getting denied access.

The ZPA admin portal > Dashboard > Application section is also populated for applications being denied by Access Policies.

Cons of having "Forward to ZPA" as the default policy action:

The users cannot access some local domains/IP addresses that match ZPA App Segment definitions.

Please reach out to us in the comments section if you have any questions.

## AD/DC Enumeration via ZPA: Workflow, Prerequisites, & Best Practices

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000066An0AI/addc-enumeration-via-zpa-workflow-prerequisites-best-practices
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-04-08T12:39:57.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited April 8, 2026 at 12:39 PM

AD/DC Enumeration via ZPA: Workflow, Prerequisites, & Best Practices

Note:

Special thanks to

Zain Rafiqi

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Active Directory and Domain Controller enumeration over Zscaler Private Access

Large enterprises that run Domain Controllers (DCs) across multiple geographies typically design their Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) deployment so that:

Users are

steered to the “nearest” DC

(lowest latency) for authentication and directory queries.

AD site awareness still works (so clients land on the correct site/DC for logon and GPO).

Access is

segmented and least-privilege

, because DC protocols can be high-risk if broadly exposed.

This article outlines the

end-user workstation flow

, then maps it to a

recommended ZPA configuration

pattern

used in global environments.

Workstation flow: How AD site, logon, and GPO processing typically works

When a workstation boots, a user signs in, and Group Policy refresh occurs, the common sequence looks like this:

DC discovery and site determination

DNS SRV lookup

_ldap._tcp.domain.com (and/or _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.domain.com)

The client receives a list of DCs ordered by priority/weight.

CLDAP “site discovery” (UDP/389)

The client sends a CLDAP ping to candidate DCs from the SRV list.

The DC uses the source information to respond with the client’s AD Site (and typically indicates the most appropriate DC for that site).

LDAP / LDAPS directory operations (TCP/389 or TCP/636)

The client performs directory queries required for logon, policy, and domain operations.

Authentication (Kerberos)

DNS SRV lookup

_kerberos._tcp.domain.com

Kerberos authentication (TCP/88 and/or UDP/88)

Client obtains TGT and service tickets.

Optional: Kerberos password change (TCP/464, UDP/464).

Group Policy retrieval and SYSVOL/NETLOGON access

RPC Endpoint Mapper (TCP/135)

The client queries which dynamic RPC port to use for a given service.

Dynamic RPC (TCP high ports, typically 49152–65535 on modern Windows)

Used by various AD/GPO-related RPC interfaces.

SMB (TCP/445)

Access to \\domain.com\SYSVOL and \\domain.com\NETLOGON to download GPOs/scripts and for related domain operations.

Note:

RPC Endpoint Mapper is TCP/135 (not TCP/137). TCP/137 is NetBIOS Name Service and is generally not what you want to rely on in modern AD designs. GPO processing commonly depends heavily on SMB (445) for SYSVOL and on RPC (135 + dynamic ports) for certain management interfaces.

What “nearest DC” means in a ZPA-based design

In traditional networks, “nearest DC” is often determined by AD Sites and Services (subnets mapped to sites) plus DNS SRV weighting. With ZPA in the middle, the enterprise goal is usually:

Make the

ZPA App Connector egress

appear as the “client source” to the DCs in that region, so CLDAP site discovery returns the expected site/DC.

Ensure the user is

served by the closest App Connector Group

(which is typically in-region, close to the DCs).

This is why enterprises commonly deploy:

Regional App Connector Groups

(Americas / EMEA / APAC, etc.)

Each connector group placed into

matching AD Sites/Subnets

(from AD’s point of view)

Recommended ZPA configuration pattern (enterprise/global)

Connector Groups dedicated to AD/DC access

Create

dedicated App Connector Groups for Active Directory

(separate from generic app connector groups).

Place connectors

close to DCs

(same region/DC LAN where possible).

Ensure App Connectors can reach DCs on required ports.

Ensure the

App Connector IPs

belong to the correct

AD Sites and Services subnets

so AD site logic remains meaningful.

Dynamic Server Discovery (DSD) for “closest connector group”

Create a

Dynamic Server Discovery group for Active Directory

that includes all

AD-dedicated Connector Groups

Associate your DC-related application segments with this DSD group so ZPA can choose the best connector group for the user (typically based on proximity/latency and policy).

Application Segments strategy (keep it structured, not overly broad)

DC-specific application segments (recommended)

Create application segments that include

Domain Controller FQDNs

(or a DC server group) and explicitly permit only the required ports.

Wildcard segment for domain FQDN routing (use carefully)

Some designs use a wildcard (e.g., *.domain.com) so name-based flows remain consistent.

If you do this, keep it

tightly controlled

(who can access it, what ports, and whether it’s only for DC-related hostnames).

Avoid “allow almost everything to *.domain.com” unless you have strong compensating controls.

AD/DC port set (map to your real needs)

Below is a common set that enterprises start from, then prune based on use case:

Function

Protocol/Port

Kerberos

TCP/88, UDP/88

Kerberos password change

TCP/464, UDP/464

LDAP

TCP/389, UDP/389 (UDP used for CLDAP)

LDAPS (recommended)

TCP/636

Global Catalog

TCP/3268

Global Catalog SSL (optional)

TCP/3269

RPC Endpoint Mapper

TCP/135

Dynamic RPC

TCP/49152–65535

(or your defined RPC range)

SMB (SYSVOL/NETLOGON)

TCP/445

NTP (only if required/desired)

UDP/123

Practical hardening tip: If possible,

define a reduced dynamic RPC range

on DCs/servers and permit only that range instead of 49152–65535.

Why “include all connector groups” on DC segments matters (your key point, tightened)

Your main objective is correct and worth highlighting more explicitly:

The client sends CLDAP pings (UDP/389) to multiple DCs returned by DNS SRV.

You want those CLDAP requests to

egress from the appropriate regional App Connector

so the DC’s site logic responds with the

site-correct DC

By associating the DC application segment with a DSD group that contains

all regional AD connector groups

, ZPA can select the connector group that is “closest” to the user and therefore keeps site/DC affinity aligned.

This is the core mechanism that helps global enterprises keep

AD performance optimal

and

DC selection predictable

without backhauling user traffic across the world.

Please reach out to us in the comments section if you have any questions.

(Partner)

## How to create additional root-level account on App Connector for ZPA

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000066M50AI/how-to-create-additional-rootlevel-account-on-app-connector-for-zpa
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-04-13T15:17:22.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited April 13, 2026 at 3:17 PM

How to create additional root-level account on App Connector for ZPA

Note:

Special thanks to

Gaurav Jaswal

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

Customers might need to create an additional privileged, root-level account on a Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) App Connector. A common scenario for this requirement is providing a Vulnerability Assessment (VA) team with the necessary access to perform security scans on the host operating system (OS).

Solution

When you deploy an App Connector on a custom Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) host using the Red Hat Package Manager (RPM), you are responsible for managing the OS-level accounts. Standard security policies often require unique accounts for different administrative tasks rather than sharing a single root credential.

Managing your own OS accounts is a standard part of maintaining a custom RHEL-based host. You can create additional users with sudo privileges as long as these accounts do not interfere with Zscaler processes or system resources.

To create a separate root-level user account on an App Connector running on a custom OS, complete the following steps:

Create the new user and assign a bash shell:

sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash

sudo passwd

Grant administrative rights by adding the user to the wheel group:

sudo usermod -aG wheel

Confirm that the new user has the correct sudo access:

sudo -l -U

Note

: Always follow your organization's internal security guidelines regarding password complexity and account rotation when creating new privileged users.

Please reach out to us in the comments if you have any questions.

## How to migrate ZPA Policy Enforcement from SAML Attributes to SCIM Attributes

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000066Nh0AI/how-to-migrate-zpa-policy-enforcement-from-saml-attributes-to-scim-attributes
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-04-10T12:53:49.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited April 10, 2026 at 12:53 PM

How to migrate ZPA Policy Enforcement from SAML Attributes to SCIM Attributes

Note:

Special thanks to

Zain Rafiqi

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

This article describes a safe migration path to move ZPA policy enforcement from SAML assertion attributes to SCIM-provisioned attributes/groups, minimizing user impact and providing a rollback option.

To complete this migration you have meet the follow prerequisites:

ZPA integrated with an IdP (e.g., Okta, Azure AD) using SAML for authentication.

SCIM provisioning configured or planned for ZPA.

Admin access to:

ZPA Admin Portal (IdP Configuration, Policy)

IdP provisioning settings (SCIM)

Solution

Phase 1 — Prep and Validate (before any policy change)

Enable SCIM Sync and let it fully populate

In ZPA, enable SCIM Sync for your IdP.

Allow time for full population (48 hours to 1 week, depending on tenant size and sync cadence).

Validate:

Users and groups exist on SCIM Users / SCIM Groups pages.

Users show as Active in SCIM Sync Logs.

Confirm SCIM userName matches SAML NameID

Requirement: SCIM userName must equal the SAML NameID used for login.

Why it matters: A mismatch can block logins and cause an outage when policies begin relying on SCIM identity.

If you change usernames:

Have users log out and log back in to Zscaler Client Connector (ZCC) to re-register and regenerate the client certificate.

Okta-specific (recommended) full sync hardening

Enable PROVISION_OUT_OF_SYNC_USERS.

Then unassign/reassign users/groups to force a full sync into ZPA before enabling SCIM policy enforcement.

This helps prevent ZCC “connection error” during reauthentication/reauth flows.

Phase 2 — Pre-stage Policies (no behavior change yet)

The goal is to stage SCIM criteria into existing rules without changing enforcement until you are ready.

Add SCIM equivalents with OR logic

For each policy rule currently using SAML attributes:

Add the equivalent SCIM attribute or SCIM group using OR.

Example:

SAML dept = X OR SCIM dept = X

Important behavior note (during staging):

While SCIM Attributes for Policy toggle is OFF, ZPA will skip SCIM criteria in OR expressions and enforcement remains SAML-only.

Avoid using AND between SAML and SCIM during staging

Do not stage rules like: SAML dept = X AND SCIM dept = X

With SCIM enforcement disabled, the SCIM side won’t evaluate, and AND-based logic can fail unexpectedly.

Phase 3 — Enablement (controlled cutover)

Enable SCIM attributes for policy enforcement

Go to IdP Configuration in ZPA.

Enable SCIM Attributes for Policy.

User impact

Users will see a one-time reauthentication prompt.

Existing/ongoing app connections are generally not impacted.

During cutover, SAML and SCIM criteria can both work (especially with staged OR rules)

Phase 4 — Verify and Ramp

Pilot first

Start with a small pilot group.

Validate:

Access works using SCIM attributes/groups.

Pilot users appear correctly in:

SCIM Users/Groups

SCIM Sync Logs

Expand gradually

ncrease coverage in batches until fully deployed.

After stabilization: remove SAML criteria

Update rules to become SCIM-only by removing SAML criteria once confidence is high.

Operational notes

SCIM user attribute values used in policy must remain accurate and continuously synced from the IdP.

SCIM group references are ID-based and typically survive group name changes.

Rollback Plan (fast restore)

If a rollback is required:

Disable SCIM Attributes for Policy in IdP Configuration.

With staged OR rules, ZPA will resume evaluating only the SAML side (SCIM is skipped), restoring prior behavior.

Edge Considerations / Limitations

ZPA supports a fixed set of SCIM attributes for policy enforcement.

If you require custom attributes not supported via SCIM, continue using SAML assertions in policy where needed.

If a user is deleted from SCIM:

Any explicit literal usernames/emails you hard-coded into policies remain and must be cleaned up manually later.

Please reach out to us in the comments section if you have any questions.

## How to collect Packet Capture and Journal Logs on Docker App Connector

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ000000673d0AA/how-to-collect-packet-capture-and-journal-logs-on-docker-app-connector
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-04-21T12:39:17.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Cd

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited April 21, 2026 at 12:39 PM

How to collect Packet Capture and Journal Logs on Docker App Connector

Note:

Special thanks to

Subhrajit Mahi

and

Shivraj Poojary

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

In this guide, you will learn to collect:

Packet captures (PCAP) for troubleshooting network traffic

Docker container logs for the App Connector

Note

: These commands need to be run on the Docker host itself and not in the container

Solution

Step 1: Packet Capture Collection (Docket Host)

Identify the Network Interface:

Run the following command on the Docker host to list available interfaces:

> ip link show

This command shows interface names (not IP assignment details)

Note down the adapter name responsible for the traffic (example: ens5)

Capture traffic to a Specific Destination Host:

Use tcpdump to capture traffic destined to a particular host:

> sudo tcpdump -i -nves0 -w /tmp/zscaler.pcap host

Where:

is the interface identified earlier (example: ens5)

is the target host you want to filter on (example: google.com)

Output file will be saved as:

/tmp/zscaler.pcap

Refer to the example below:

sudo tcpdump -i ens5 -nves0 -w /tmp/zscaler.pcap host

google.com

If the correct interface cannot be identified:

If you are unsure which interface is carrying the traffic, capture on all interfaces, use the command below:

> sudo tcpdump -i any -nves0 -w /tmp/zscaler.pcap host

google.com

Open (Unfiltered) packet capture:

To run an open capture (no destination filter), use the command below.

> sudo tcpdump -i any -nves0 -w /tmp/zscaler.pcap

Note

: Open packet capture can generate large files quickly. Stop the capture once you reproduce the issue.

Step 2: Logs Collection (Docker Host)

Refer to the command to see running container on docker:

> sudo docker ps -a

Once you have the container ID of the App Connector:

View Recent Logs (Last 50 Lines)

: To quickly review recent container logs, use the command below.

> sudo docker logs --tail 50

Follow Logs in Real Time: To stream logs live, use the command below.

> sudo docker logs -f

Export Logs with Timestamps to a File:

To export logs with timestamps into a file for sharing, use the commands below.

> sudo docker logs -t > /tmp/log.txt

Refer to the outputs collect below:

Packet capture file:

/tmp/zscaler.pcap

Docker logs file (optional export):

/tmp/log.txt

You can view the file by using the command below:

#cd /tmp

#ls

It will show you the captured file. You can use winscp or other tools to export the collected log files from the docker host.

The below steps will help you to pull rotated or archived journal logs which includes all zpa-connector-child events:

Access the Linux instance console where the Docker App Connector container is running.

Run

sudo docker ps

to list the App Connector container details, as shown below:

Note the App Connector container ID where you like to grab the logs, then navigate to

/var/lib/docker/containers

using

cd

as shown below:

Run the command

ls -l

to list the container log directories, as shown below:

Identify the folder that corresponds to the container you are troubleshooting. The directory name starts with the full unique container ID.

For example, the folder - "

085dc01a5c1ce2933a4384fdf48afe68527da4eea41e840960d250f09ed2faab

" matches the App Connector container ID "

085dc01a5c1c

", as shown below:

Run

cd

command to get into the required container folder and collect all files that include `json.log` in the filename, as shown below:

Please reach out to us in the comments if you have any questions.

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000006BYf0AM/deploying-private-service-edge-pse-in-docker-using-a-static-iphost-ip-address

(Employee) posted a Guide

Deploying Private Service Edge (PSE) in Docker using a static IP/host IP address

Note:

Special thanks to

Prabhjot Singh

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

When deploying a Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) Private Service Edge (PSE) using Docker, you might need to assign a static IP address or use the host machine's network. This guide walks you through the necessary steps to successfully deploy a PSE container with these specific networking requirements.

Solution

Removing the existing container

If you have already deployed a container but need to switch to a host IP address, you must remove the existing container. There is no way to change the IP address of a running container in a persistent manner.

To safely stop and remove the existing container, complete these steps:

1. Stop the running container using the following command:

docker stop zpa-service-edge

2. Remove the container using the following command:

docker rm zpa-service-edge

Understanding Docker networking

By default, Docker containers receive assigned IP addresses from the default Docker network subnet, which is typically 172.17.0.0/16. If you want to assign a container a static IP outside of this default subnet and ensure the IP address persists across reboots, you must create a Docker bridge network. A bridge network provides isolation while still allowing containers to communicate with each other on the same host.

Creating a new Docker bridge network

Use the following command to create a new Docker bridge network with your preferred subnet and gateway:

When running this command, ensure you provide your specific network details:

Replace with <

subnet ip>

your desired subnet.

Replace with [

gw ip

the gateway IP for the subnet.

Replace with [

network_name

your preferred network name.

Note:

If you plan to use the host network instead of a bridge network, you can skip this step. The host network configuration does not require you to create a custom network.

Creating a new PSE container with a static IP

Use the following command to create a new container with the configured network and static IP address:

When running this command, ensure you provide your specific configuration details:

Replace [

network_name

with the name of the bridge network you created in the previous step.

Replace [

static ip

]with the desired static IP address for this container.

Using the host network

Alternatively, if you are using the host network rather than a bridge network, use the following command to create a new container:

Note:

When using the host network, a static IP cannot be directly assigned to the container. Instead, the container uses an IP address from the host machine's network.

Verifying the deployment

After creating the container, it is important to confirm your configuration is working properly. Complete these steps to verify your deployment:

1. Confirm that the container is running with the correct static IP address using the following command:

docker inspect zpa-service-edge

2. Verify that the ZPA App Connector container has been successfully deployed using the following command:

docker ps

By following these steps, you should be able to successfully deploy the PSE in Docker with a static IP address or using the host network.

Refer the following documentation

https://help.zscaler.com/zpa/private-service-edge-deployment-guide-docker

to learn more about advanced deployment options.

Please reach out to us in the comments if you have any questions.

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000006BiL0AU/how-to-configure-a-static-ip-address-on-a-newly-deployed-rhel9-zpa-app-connector

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

May 29, 2026 at 12:40 PM

How to configure a static IP address on a newly deployed RHEL9 ZPA App Connector

Note:

Special thanks to

Subhrajit Mahi

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

Setting up a static Internet Protocol (IP) address ensures reliable and consistent connectivity for your App Connector. You can quickly make this change using the built-in network management tool in the console.

Solution

To configure a static IP address for your App Connector:

Log in to the App Connector console

Run the following command:

sudo nmtui

Enter the password

Open the connection editor

In the blue nmtui screen, select Edit a connection.

Select and edit the appropriate network interface.

Use arrow keys to highlight the interface.

Choose Edit and press Enter.

Set IPv4 to Manual and enter details

Change IPv4 Configuration from Automatic to Manual.

Click Show to reveal configuration fields.

Add the IP Address, Gateway, and DNS Server details. For e.g.- IP Address: 10.10.10.50/24, Gateway: 10.10.10.1, and DNS Server: 8.8.8.8 / 8.8.4.4

Apply changes

Save the configuration.

Exit nmtui. Select > back > enter

Restart NetworkManager by running the following command:

sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager

Verify the IP assignment by running the following command and confirm the static IP is applied:

ip a s

If the IP is not correctly applied, then reboot the App Connector by running the following command:

sudo reboot.

Follow step 7 and verify the IP assignment.

Please reach out to us in the comments if you have any questions.

Use Application Segment Import to create an application segment through CSV file

Note:

Special thanks to

Rohit Bisht

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

You can efficiently add multiple applications to your network by importing a CSV file into the Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) Admin Portal. Before importing, it needs to be ensured that the CSV file contains these headers in sequential order:

Application Name

Application FQDN/IP

TCP Ports

UDP Ports

App Owner

Contact

Application Importance

Hosting Location

Environment

These specific fields are mandatory and cannot be empty:

Application Name

Application FQDN/IP

TCP Ports or UDP Ports

You can leave the remaining fields empty if they do not apply to your configuration. If you need to include multiple ports, use a hyphen between the values to indicate a port range (e.g. 1-52).

Example of CSV file:

Solution

Adding the application segment

To add your application segments using the prepared CSV file:

Create the CSV file with valid headers and values.

Import the CSV file to the ZPA Admin Portal.

Select the checkbox as shown below

Click Actions and select Add Application Segments.

Select the Segment Group and Server Group from your existing configuration on the ZPA Admin Portal.

Click Add Application Segment at the bottom of the page to finalize adding the segment.

To learn more about importing application segments, review these articles:

About Application Segment Import

Using Application Segment Import

Please reach out to us in the comments if you have any questions.

## Changing your Windows password during a privileged remote access RDP Session

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000006X2v0AE/changing-your-windows-password-during-a-privileged-remote-access-rdp-session
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-07-21T12:47:58.000Z

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited 19h ago

Changing your Windows password during a privileged remote access RDP Session

Note:

Special thanks to

Subhrajit Mahi

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

This article describes the step-by-step procedure to change a Windows user password while connected to a remote desktop via ZPA Privileged Remote Access (PRA). The process involves using the on-screen keyboard within the PRA session toolbar to send the Ctrl + Alt + Del command to the remote machine, then using the standard Windows "Change a password" option.

Solution

To change your Windows password during an active PRA RDP session, follow the steps below.

While connected to the PRA RDP session, click the Keyboard icon on the top toolbar. This opens the on-screen keyboard.

On the on-screen keyboard, select Ctrl + Alt + Del. This displays the Windows security options on the remote machine, including: Lock, Switch User, Sign out, Change a password, and Task Manager.

Click Change a password.

Enter your current password, then type and confirm your new password — just as you would on a standard Windows device.

Once the password has been changed successfully, end the session to log out of the remote machine.

Rejoin the session using the Join option and sign in with your new password to confirm the change was successful.

Note:

The on-screen keyboard is required because the local operating system captures Ctrl + Alt + Del before it can be sent to the remote session. Using the on-screen keyboard routes the input directly to the remote machine.

Please reach out to us in the comments if you require any further assistance.
